items.note: Story 1: Association named, organized 1889 at Larrow Green, creamery 1891. Gideon-as-first-president appears only in B3 (no travel into A), but this list-type item with no REQUIRED line takes its core fact.
Article VII quoted verbatim in Story 1, including 'the test of the station where he delivers shall govern'.

Never states that the rule is what made a wrong test cost money; Story 1 says only that the clause 'locked each station's test as the authoritative measure, with no appeal or cross-check' and calls it 'fateful'. The significance is argued in B3, which cannot travel into A.
Story 4 gives Loomis secretary from 1901 and keeper of the minute book, Teague bookkeeper from 1905. Sill is not named as buttermaker inside A, but the core fact is carried.
Story 3 gives Selby Vose manager from 1913; 'Gideon's son' appears only in B3. Core fact of a list-type item credited; the nephew corruption is never asserted.

Story 4 gives the 'station gain' line, its shape (more fat arriving than the station's books bought), about five and a quarter per cent, carried to the general account. Origin misdated to 1905 — deducted separately, not scored here.

Story 1 asserts the station 'opened on May 1, 1897' — neither bolded element earned: no 4 May 1896 opening and no glassware borrowed from Larrow Green anywhere in Section A. The correct resolution appears only in Section E (Conflict 6), which cannot travel into A.
The bench system is never described in Section A: no weighing at intake, no composite sample, no percent read on the graduated neck after a fixed charge from the pipette, no cream-down/skim-back.
Story 1: outfit from Ammon & Sons of Tarnet on the invoice of 14 April 1897, with Orra's diary for 1 May 1897 ('station's own glass came up') in the same story.
Six dozen pipettes blown to 17.6 c.c., bottles, acid measure, hand tester, freight, $77.93.

Nowhere in Section A is the shortfall said to be flat — the same 0.19 in every month, flush and feeding alike, for twenty-six years. The year-round claim appears only in Section F, and Section F then garbles Alder Corners into a summer-versus-winter comparison.
Never states that a pipette cannot be checked without a burette, or that there was none in the county. The nearest remark is in Section D and is about 1911 routine only.
Ansel Keddie, tester for twenty-nine seasons, dismissed 30 April 1925 — the item's aspect (service and its end) carried, though the run starts him in 1897 rather than 1896.
The test book is named and attributed to Keddie's hand across the twenty-nine seasons, with entries quoted; bold gates on the test book.
Both figures required. The summary leaf's 1896 = 3.80 never appears in Section A; only the 3.61 average and a 1922 leaf quotation about the 1911 interval.
Story 5: broke 8 May, borrowed measure to 10 July, nine weeks at 3.80, back to 3.61 the day the station's own measure returned, with Keddie's question mark.
Orra is his wife (diary), Emmet is her brother, and Emmet is the station's largest patron — all inside Section A (Stories 3 and 7).
1919 circular over the manager's signature (Story 3) and the 17 March 1925 statement quoted: tested as taught, could not tell why the figures were what they were, never took a pound of cream.
Story 7: died 1934 with the imputation on him.
Hessel Bottom a wet meadow, six farms with rights, Emmet Brant's the largest (Stories 1, 2, 7).
Neither the 1 January 1897 start of Brant's private weigh book nor the agreement of the two scales appears in Section A; both are in Section C2 only.

The 1902 complaints are stated, but the item's gate is failed: Story 1 and Story 2 both give the Hollow-vs-Green comparison as '0.17 to 0.19', conflating the visible 0.17 gap with the 0.19 true shortfall. The key charges this loss to the solver's own arithmetic.
Grigg's 1908 committee, Jan-Feb-Mar sampling, and the wet-hay conclusion given as the report's opinion, not as fact; Bulletin 214 is used against it in the same story.
Brant's 1910 year (200,000 lb on a recorded 3.42) appears only in Section C2; nothing on proportional loss or the richer herds losing more appears in Section A.
Story 8's document list: 'Roy Brant's weigh book (lent to Ivy summer 1958)'.
Inside Section A only 'Alder Corners test book' and 'Rosalie Cudd' appear. Redlow Ridge, Vessey County and Jerome Cudd are named only in Section F3.
Neither 1915 nor the summer-flush haulage appears in Section A.
REQUIRED two of four independence elements. Section A names the artifact only ('Alder Corners test book'), which the key says does not carry the item on its own.
Section A says only that four farmers tested 3.78-3.82 at the factory 'vs. lower at Ostrey Hollow' — no every-overlapping-season claim, no 0.19, no sixteen seasons.
The same-milk-same-meadow-same-months argument is never made; Section F actually recasts it as summer-at-Alder-Corners against winter-at-Ostrey-Hollow, which destroys the control.

Rosalie Cudd provided copies of the Alder Corners figures to Ivy in 1958 (Story 8). 'Sixteen seasons' and 'daughter' absent, but the two bolded acts — Rosalie Cudd, copying for Ivy in 1958 — are stated.
Merle Strawn, state dairy inspector, circuit 1907-1936, detailed circuit notebooks.
Lactometer on every visit, never any water found at Ostrey Hollow, quoted from the 1919 entry and repeated at the 1923 condemnation entry.
12 June 1923, pipettes run against the burette, whole crate condemned.

Quotes 'I did not weigh what it has cost them' but never states the point — that he wrote no figure for the deficiency, made no report beyond the condemnation and drew no inference about the years behind it.
Replacement ordered 28 June, Ammon's reply 2 July 1923, new glass in use that July, 1924 tests rose to 3.80 and stayed there. 3.90 never asserted.
The crate set aside in the station loft on 12 June 1923, where it lay thirty-five years.
Patrons petitioned in January 1925.
Board under Alonzo Frick, three sittings from 17 March to the 4 May 1925 award, two of them in the station's weigh room.
All three explanations argued with their advocates — watering (Vose), theft (Teague), the 1908 hay report read in — and 'finds no cause established'.
'Exhibits presented were four books only', enumerated, including Strawn's 1923 circuit notebook.
Dismissed 30 April 1925 with Frick's 'There was no finding against him from us'; award of 4 May 1925 quoted with $3,800, 'without admission', charged to the station account.

Says the award was one fifth of the loss, but never makes the identity: nothing connects the account the award was charged to with the account into which the 'gain' had been accumulating since 1898. Story 4 in fact puts the gain in 'the general account' and leaves it there.
Ivy Keddie, Ansel's granddaughter, daughter of Duncan, graduate student in dairy husbandry at the State Agricultural College at Farland, with Vaught named.
Story 8 lists the records she brought together — the crate, Strawn's notebook, Brant's weigh book, the Alder Corners book, the college measurement.
February 1958, crate found in the loft over the intake room, nine pipettes surviving.
Measurement sheet of 9 March 1958 against a calibrated burette, mean 16.72 against a marked 17.6, short 0.88 c.c., 0.95 of the mark. 16.27 correctly rejected.
Every test 95 per cent of true from 1 May 1897 to 12 June 1923 (Bulletin quotation), 3.61 recorded where 3.80 stood, 0.19 short.

REQUIRED all four, all right, inside Section A. The fat (76,000) and the ledger identity are there, but Section A never commits to the milk or the money: Story 4 gives '40,000,000 to 44,000,000 pounds (discrepancy between sources)' and Story 6 gives '$19,000-$19,600'. The clean 40,000,000 and $19,000 appear only in Section C.
Bulletin No. 471, October 1958, quoted, stating the cause and clearing him; 35 years after condemnation and 24 after his death given.
Granddaughter, with the Duncan-is-Ansel's-son derivation and the 'great-niece' error corrected.

Second cousins with correct derivation (+1). The abstention pole (A08) missed: what the run says the sources leave open is whether Ivy and Hazel knew each other, not whether Emmet and Orra were full or half siblings. Neither is asserted, so no -2.
Gideon Vose, his father (+1); significance stated — Gideon wrote the by-laws and Article VII made the station's test decide every patron's pay, and Selby inherited that system (+1).

'The sources cannot definitively settle this' plus a hedged lean ('the most likely answer') = correct abstention under the operational test, no -2. States what is established: talk on one side, a family member's flat denial on the other, no documented genealogy.
16.72 / 17.6 = 0.95; 95 per cent of true, short 5 per cent, one part in twenty.
$19,000 at 25c; award $3,800 = 20 per cent, one fifth. Both required elements given.

Gives $90.00 (360 x $0.25). The key's answer is $86.40 at the 1910 price of 24c; $90.00 is accepted only if the solver states explicitly that it is using the period average of 25c instead of the 1910 price. It never mentions 24c.
1,444,000 lb credited.
1,520,000 lb actually delivered in the cream.
Both denominators named: 76,000/1,520,000 = 5% of fat delivered; 76,000/1,444,000 = 0.0526 of fat credited. Mislabels 0.0526 as '5.25%' but does not commit the '5.26 per cent of the true fat' error.
Line items reproduced and summed to $77.93, with Junia's own $77.39 noticed and rejected.
72 pipettes (6 dozen) and 0.88 c.c. short each — both required elements.

Exact-match item. Gives '26 years, 1 month, 12 days'; the key's answer is 26 years and 6 weeks, with 26 years 42 days or 26 years 1 month 11 days accepted. 1 May 1897 to 12 June 1923 is 11 days, not 12. The 25 full years 1898-1922 and the reason for the difference are correct, but the duration figure is not.

Abstention A02 correctly declined — 'exact figure cannot be determined from sources' — with both poles and the reason the record is missing. Story 1's 900,000 is attributed to Sill's recollection and qualified, so no -2.
Variable named: the measuring pipette, broken 8 May, borrowed measure to 10 July.
Constants well beyond three: herds, cows, season, pasture, farms, tester's hands, acid, bottles, protocol.
3.80 through the nine weeks, back to 3.61 on 10 July; 'six weeks' explicitly rejected.
Both halves: isolates the glass and eliminates feed, weather, management and operator honesty; and states limits — no mechanism, no direct measurement of the defect, no verdict on intent.
Three reasons attributed to three narrators/documents: the 1911 interval (Keddie's test book), Teague's own station-gain ledger, Sill's weighing of the cream at reception.

The 1958-independence half is stated, but the mutual-independence showing fails: reasons 2 and 3 rest on the same event — the cream arriving heavy at Larrow Green — which the key's own list treats as one reason. Both halves are required.
Abstention A09 asserted. Verdict sentence: 'Did Teague question the ledger entries? No.', with the 1916 report to Vose then asserted as fact. -2 applied.
Answers the literal question yes, on the 1919 circular and the 1926 address.
REQUIRED three of five met: manager from 1913, signed the annual sheets carrying the station-gain line, wrote the 1919 water circular, argued watering at the 1925 hearing.

No declared inability to settle whether he knew the tests were understated; only 'whether he understood the cause is unclear', and none of the five supporting observations is offered as ground for suspending judgment. Its verdict stays in item-1 territory ('tests ran low'), so no -2 under the key's discriminating rule.

Capped at 3. Found, resolved and methodised: the award ($3,800 against Oram's $3,500); the condemnation date (12 June against Rundle's 12 July); the surviving pipettes (nine against Rundle's eleven). A fourth eligible resolution beyond the cap: Kyle's 1 May 1898 glass date rejected against the 1897 invoice.

NT-12: names Kepp and Roy Brant as both carrying 'six weeks' — a dedicated section headed 'Two narrators repeating same wrong value' — and breaks it on Keddie's dated entries. NT-1: names Bulletin 471 and the Ashlin Chronicle as both carrying 16.27 and breaks it on Ivy's measurement sheet. No third pair is identified as a pair.
No abstention conflict earned. A04 and A06 are never raised; A10 is not raised as a conflict and 1891 is asserted flatly in Story 1.
Identifies Junia Ammon refuting herself on the page: her firm history says $77.39 while the invoice she reproduces sums to $77.93.

Names the pipettes of the 1897 crate, 16.72 against a marked 17.6, 95 per cent of true; states the error is proportional rather than a constant; gives onset (in use 1 May 1897) and cessation (condemned 12 June 1923, 1924 average 3.80).
Watering named to Selby Vose and defeated by Strawn's lactometer on every visit and by the 1911 interval.
Theft named to Teague and defeated by the cream arriving heavy in Teague's own ledger and in Sill's weighing.

Bog hay named to Grigg's 1908 committee and Kepp, and defeated by Bulletin 214's five hundredths in winter and nothing in summer against a 0.19 gap. Its Alder Corners leg is mangled into a summer/winter comparison, but Bulletin 214 carries the item.
Abstention A07 asserted: 'No. ... The board never examined the glass and never knew to test it.' -2 applied.
Abstention A05 asserted: 'Ansel suspected the glass.' as the opening verdict, on Duncan's single uncorroborated recollection. -2 applied.
178 words against a 150-word cap; the sheet's own count of 149 is wrong.
Three record series only — the Association's ledgers, Strawn's testing, the 1958 measurement. Five required.
No decoy adopted as fact and no wrong headline figure: 3.61, 3.80, 76,000, $19,000, 5 per cent, nine weeks all correct.
Four of six with both ends covered: 5 per cent low and 1897 at the onset, 1958 at the close, 76,000 lb / $19,000, and both Keddies named.

deductions.reason: Corruption: asserts the station-gain line was invented by Teague in 1905 ('In 1905, Wilbur Teague ... invented an accounting line he called station gain', repeated in D2 as 'his ledger line -- which he created in 1905'). The line was carried from 1898; r05's 'my own device, from 1905' is a catalogued planted error.
Corruption: asserts the 1919 circular reached eleven families — the run's own Quantities line, 'Ansel personally delivered to eleven families'. The circular's reach was nine.

Corruption: asserts 67,000 lb and $19,600 as live values for the loss in Story 6 ('The patrons' own reckoning was 67,000 to 76,000 pounds ... equaling $19,000-$19,600'; Quantities: 'one-fifth of actual loss ($19,000-$19,600 total)'), unhedged and in the sheet's own voice.
Gullibility: abstention item A05 answered with a definite assertion — 'Ansel suspected the glass.' (Section F).
Gullibility: abstention item A07 answered with a definite assertion — 'No. ... The board never examined the glass' (Section F).
Gullibility: abstention item A09 answered with a definite assertion — 'Did Teague question the ledger entries? No.', with the 1916 report to Vose asserted as fact (Section D2).
Gullibility: abstention item A10 answered with a definite assertion — 'In 1891, the main creamery opened, introducing payment by weight of butter fat' (Story 1), stated with no attribution or hedge.
